newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST-Energy price dip to limit U.S. March PPI.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Energy price dip to limit U.S. March PPI.

text.p: Declining energy prices and a smoothly running manufacturing sector should keep the March U.S. Producer Price Index (PPI) in check, supporting a view of tame near-term wholesale inflation, experts said on Wednesday.

The report, set for release Friday at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT, was expected to show the overall PPI was unchanged in March and the core PPI, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, rose 0.1 percent, according to a Reuters poll.
That compares with a 0.4-percent overall decline and 0.1-percent core decline in February.
Deflation in the energy sector will offer the strongest restraint on wholesale prices, said Christopher Low, senior economist at HSBC Markets Inc.
"You still have prices falling in the energy sector, particularly oil and gas prices," he said. "That alone should give you a flat headline number."
Overall PPI might record another decline if natural gas and residential electricity prices fall as well, an event forecast by some economists.
While core PPI is expected to rise, the absence of any particular spikes should limit its gains to one or possibly two tenths of a percentage point, economists said.

"There were very few signs in any recent PPI reports of bubbling inflation in the manufacturing sector," said David Kelly, senior economist at Primark Decision Economics. "It's unlikely we're going to see a big pop in finished goods."
PPI's indicators of future inflation -- crude and intermediate goods prices -- prompted more of a debate among analysts, but none predicted shocking news.
Crude items prices fell 5.9 percent in February against a 5.2-percent January increase, and intermediates declined 0.1 percent last month versus a 0.2-percent rise the month before.
But some experts viewed February as an anomaly and suggested keeping a close watch for any increases in non-finished items.

"The intermediate and crude goods prices have been rising for a while," Low said. "That's where you've got the hints that the good news in the finished goods ex-food and -energy isn't going to last that much longer."
The fixed-income market may not exhibit a large reaction if the data emerge as expected, economists said.
Friday's retail sales report and next Tuesday's consumer price report command the near-term focus.

The report "probably won't do much to lift the market unless it's a lot better (than expected)" said Stuart Hoffman, chief economist at PNC Bank Corp. "It would have to show some declines in the total and in the core rate."
Central bankers, too, will only briefly set their gaze on March producer prices, preferring instead to concentrate on wage-related inflation and on future price trend expectations, economists said.
"I don't see where this really changes the Fed's focus and it won't add much to the debate about what the Fed's going to do next," Hoffman said.
